evidence: Screens show flower pots/rows that are tapped strictly 'in order' left-to-right, with the running total displayed underneath (e.g. '4', then '4, 8') - this is a linear reveal sequence, not a puzzle; a child tapping pots in the only visible left-to-right order will always succeed regardless of whether they understand skip-counting.

The transition from equal-groups pots to the array screen simply re-renders the same flower count (4 per group, same total) as rows - visually pleasant but the interaction is identical (tap in order, see count appear underneath), so the 'array' concept is asserted via text ('This is called an array') rather than demonstrated through any structural change in how the child interacts with the rows vs columns.
critique: The garden theme (sunflowers, orange gradient sky, sun) is warm and cohesive, and the pacing that moves from equal-groups pots to arrays is a reasonable curricular sequence. But the actual interaction at every step observed is the same shallow pattern: tap the next item in a fixed left-to-right order, watch a number appear, watch a running tally build underneath. There is no moment where the child must reason about grouping, no drag-to-arrange, no choice between correct/incorrect groupings, no self-directed 'build your own' construction visible in the trace despite the button being labeled 'Next: Build my own!' — the trace shows only a '+' tap tested on the following screen with no visible resulting screenshot of a constructed array to confirm the builder actually works meaningfully. The array screen's core promise — that rows and columns reveal multiplication structure differently than loose equal groups — is never made tangible; the rows are tapped exactly the same way the pots were tapped, with identical skip-count-and-total feedback. This matches the calibration pattern for 'attractive scenery around ordinary tap targets': pretty flowers with a rigid, order-dependent tap sequence rather than genuine spatial/structural engagement with rows vs. columns. Nothing here rises to the level of Skyglider or Comet Trail's integrated, visually-central math action; it also isn't as bad as the harbor costume example since the flowers do stay on screen and the numbers displayed are accurate and pedagogically relevant, but the mechanic itself is answer-button-equivalent (tap targets in sequence) dressed in garden art. The word-problem interpretation and true array/rows-vs-columns contrast promised in the concept are not demonstrated with evidence in the trace beyond a label change from 'pots' to 'rows.'
